hook: The gladiator who led a slave army against Rome.

pages.x: Spartacus came from Thrace, in the Balkans. He may have served with the Roman army, deserted and been caught, and was sold as a slave. He was trained as a gladiator at a school in Capua, to fight, and often die, for the entertainment of crowds.

In 73 BC about 70 gladiators broke out of the school, armed with kitchen knives and spits, and seized a cart of weapons. They camped on Mount Vesuvius. When a Roman force blocked the only path down, they climbed down the cliffs on ropes of wild vines and attacked from behind.

Runaway slaves and poor farmers flocked to him until his army numbered 70,000 or more. He beat one Roman army after another and marched north towards the Alps and freedom. Then, for reasons no one knows, the rebels turned back south.

Rome sent Marcus Crassus, its richest man, with eight legions. In 71 BC, before the final battle in southern Italy, Spartacus is said to have killed his own horse: if he won he would have plenty, and if he lost he would need none. He died fighting, and his body was never found.

Crassus crucified 6,000 captured rebels along the Appian Way, the road from Capua to Rome: one every 30 metres or so, for 200 kilometres. They were left there for years as a warning to every slave in Italy.

Spartacus led the largest slave revolt Rome ever faced. He became a hero to rebels and reformers: Karl Marx called him "the most splendid fellow in all of ancient history", and a famous film told his story in 1960.
pts: Led the greatest slave revolt against Rome
A symbol of the fight for freedom
